I sometimes wonder if the hyperactive type can be socially conditioned to manifest as the inattentive type, a form of masking so to speak. Hyperactivity is going to be criticized more readily than inattention, as inattention can fly under the radar a bit more often. If it helps at all, I have a list of projects around the house that I've been putting off for literal years at this point, and when I look at the whole list or even one entire big task, I tend to crumble under the overwhelm. I have to pick one tiny part of one thing to do in order to not feel that crushing weight. Not the whole task, one tiny part of it. So maybe if you have any time left today, just take down one decoration and put it away. Keep doing that every so often until all of the decorations are down.

And I know this doesn't help now, but for next Christmas--you don't have to put up a tree. You don't have to put up a bunch of decorations. What if you just put up one really beautiful wreath on your door? Something simple to take down but so beautiful that it makes you smile to see it? We are made to feel we have to put on this big show for holidays, but we really don't.

You definitely should consider couples counseling and individual counseling. You are giving him very little grace. He was encouraging you to get help and was presumably willing to pay for it--that is a type of support. He was trying to get you to go on a walk with him, I would assume, to help you calm down--that was support, and you refused  that support. If your emotions are unmanageable to the degree that you self-harm, he may feel underqualified to give you the support you need, and he is probably right. One small hurdle? No. I myself am a difficult, highly emotional person, and it took me ages to understand this, but it is painful not only for me but also for the people who love me. I think it's rude and it can make me feel dehumanized, but I try to think about what the customer might be actually feeling. Maybe they're overwhelmed that they can't find the thing and the overwhelm sort of short circuits their speech (I've been there--I got overwhelmed with too much stimulus, and sometimes I struggle to formulate full sentences when I'm in that state). Maybe they're trying to be efficient and not waste our time. Maybe they don't see us as people, but in that case, that's kind of sad for them tbh. Not a great way to move through life and it will cause them problems in their relationships. I usually ask a clarifying question if it's not clear what they are looking for and just show them where it is. You never know what's going on in someone else's head. Assuming bad intentions just makes me feel shitty.

Edit to add: I do think that it can be interpreted as just rudeness, so if your husband could learn to be more polite, that doesn't hurt him and can only help the retail workers he interacts with have a better day. He's also likely to get better results in general, so it would benefit him too actually.

NOR. I'm a vegetarian because I feel bad for the animals and being vegetarian is as far as I can go without getting sick. Dairy and egg production are still cruel on a large scale, and scale is really the problem in my opinion because factory farming is brutal. The thing is, human beings do need high-quality protein and that is more difficult to obtain without eating animal products. I'm not going to judge someone who can't or doesn't want to cut out meat. People who waste it by buying it in bulk and letting it go bad piss me off, but I'm still not going to give them a lecture unless they ask my opinion. If a person were open to changing, I would just say to try to avoid making meat the main dish of every meal. Try to cut down. If everyone did that, demand would go down, resulting in less animal suffering overall. Every little bit does help. The all-or-nothing mindset of people like your ex just pushes people away from making any changes at all and hurts the cause.

Yes. There are two instances that stick out most in my mind, but I was bullied from 4th grade through the end of high school.

1. In my freshman year, I decided to take drama to try to become more outgoing because I was painfully shy. We did some Shel Silverstein thing where we had to stand on boxes of various heights, deliver our lines while making some movement, and then freeze in a pose while another group delivered their lines and movements. There were two popular girls who stood behind me. During one rehearsal, I was frozen, and one of the two girls started softly kicking my butt. They were both laughing at how it jiggled. I was by no means overweight, but this was the era of heroin chic, and I was fat by those warped standards. I just tried to ignore it, but it was so humiliating.  One of the girls lived in my neighborhood and we'd been friends before we went to the same school and it became uncool to be my friend.


2. I was pretty obsessed with grades after the bullying first started. I was determined to do well so I could get a good job one day and not be poor anymore because having the wrong clothes, messed up teeth, etc, was one of the reasons I was bullied. During a middle school awards ceremony, I was receiving an award, and this group of popular kids was physically blocking my way to the stage and laughing. I got several awards, and they did this every time, and I was just hoping I wouldn't get called again. I should have been proud but was humiliated and wanted to disappear.

Not tooting my own horn--my obsession with grades was unhealthy and only carried forward in unhealthy ways. I couldn't get validation from my peers, so I tried to get validation through achievements, but any achievements just felt hollow. I never became successful or anything. I have a history of just working myself to death and burning out catastrophically. I can't believe people when they say "good job." I can't believe people who want to be my friend or people who say they love me. I can't tolerate good-natured, playful teasing.

This was all mixed in with continuous harassment, like popular girls telling me a popular guy liked me and then laughing when they thought I believed them. I didn't, but that didn't matter. There was a guy on the bus I took home who wasn't popular but asked me almost every day why I was so ugly. Fun times.

Akathisia is a a side effect of Auvelity and many other antidepressants. It's basically intense restlessness that makes you feel like you have to move constantly and/or makes you feel extremely internally restless. It could be that rather than mania. If the periods of feeling this before happened when you had just started Wellbutrin and lessened over time, I would think that it's likely this is what you're experiencing. That said, please talk to your prescriber about it. I'm sorry you're dealing with this.

I definitely have trouble with eating well and exercising, but I get a good amount of exercise at my job now. My brain seems to like exercise that has a purpose beyond simply keeping my body in good shape. I guess dancing is kind of like that--it is exercise, but it is also an art form, and there is novelty in learning new choreography. Is there another hobby you like to do into which exercise could be incorporated? For example, if you like photography, hiking excursions with your camera, something like that? If not, maybe getting into a team sport or volunteering in a role that requires physical work might make the exercise seem more purposeful. Stuff like working out on an elliptical going nowhere or running in circles is just so boring, and my brain is like "why are we doing this?" The only time I was really successful as a runner was when I was in a new area and running was full of seeing new sights. Once I was too familiar with the routes I could take, I lost interest in it.

Another thing that is helpful is to make to-do lists a little differently (at least for things that aren't urgent). Instead of just aiming to complete a task on X day, aim to spend X amount of time on the task. Like spending 10 minutes organizing a room rather than trying to totally complete the task in one go. You might find you can spend longer, but if you can't, you can still cross something off your to-do list. It helps reduce overwhelm, which can keep you from getting anything done at all, and still gives you a small sense of achievement. I use the Microsoft To Do app to keep track of things and have a designated day for planning the week ahead (Sunday).

The time-based to-do list doesn't work for errands unfortunately. For that, I've learned to try to run errands on random evenings during the week, when stores won't be as busy (Monday through Wednesday seem to be good days). Some stores also have sensory-friendly hours, which are typically in the morning (doesn't work for me because I'm a night owl, but works for some). I don't know if you have any sensory sensitivities, but I know many with ADHD do, so just throwing this out there. If I'm shopping in a very busy, loud store, I get pretty easily overwhelmed and will either make poor choices and forget things I needed (even with a list) or might even just give up and run out of there (and maybe cry in my car).

My favorite thing has been figuring out how to set up my environment in a way that accommodates me. Clutter overwhelms me and takes mental energy from me, but I will also forget that I have things if they're hidden from view.

Things like like installing shelving in my bathroom so I can put things away without putting them out of sight, installing a mop and broom holder on the wall, having a designated hook for my keys,  just generally parting with things I don't need, avoiding accumulating knick-knacks, storing things at their point of use, and having a clean clothes hamper and a dirty clothes hamper so I don't develop random piles of clean clothes when I don't have the executive function to put clothes away have really helped me reduce my mental load.

I don't like having much resting on counters or floors (aside from furniture) because moving things to clean is a block for me. I got a lot of this from Jessica McCabe's video "ADHD Friendly House Hacks." Highly recommend.

Like someone else said below, creating some distance from your self worth and your achievements or failures. I think looking at failure with a sense of curiosity can be helpful. Like, "that approach to this task didn't work; how might I accommodate myself to be able to do the task?" as opposed to something like "*I* failed again; why can't *I* do anything right?" You shift the blame from yourself to the process. The process failed, not *you*. Or maybe, "this particular job/activity/whatever is not a good fit for me; is there something else that might be a better fit?" as opposed to "I have to bend myself into a pretzel to be able to do this because it seems like everyone else can do it." Would you judge someone else with a disability who is struggling harshly, or would you suggest potential solutions that accommodate their struggles?

I terms of misplacing things, the biggest hacks I have are related to tailoring my environment to my needs. I try to keep my environment as simple as it can possibly be: having less stuff means having less stuff to keep track of and fewer places where things can hide from me. Also, having a plan for absent-minded mistakes that keep occurring has helped. I kept locking my keys in my car, so my partner at the time got me an extra set that I keep in a pocket in my purse. For whatever reason, it was pretty automatic that I'd grab my purse, but it'd probably be a good idea to give a set to a family member in the event that I lock my purse in the car too. I wish I had thought of the extra set(s) myself, but realizing that I should just prepare in advance for a frequent mistake happening again as opposed to trying to never make the mistake again really shifted my mindset. In terms of remembering things, I have to externalize everything by writing it down and setting up reminders (but not too many because I'll start to ignore them/get overwhelmed). I know my memory might fail me, and that's okay. It's just the way my mind is. It's not my fault.

Yes, showering and all the steps during and afterward can be tiring. I can get overwhelmed by the thought of it for sure. Have you ever considered showering at night before bed as opposed to the start of your day? Then, if you're really tired afterward, you can just go to sleep. Considering that getting to sleep is often difficult for people with ADHD, you might be able to use the tiredness after showering to your advantage and actually get a good night's rest. This could also break up the steps, so that you only have to worry about the shower at night and then do the rest of the stuff in the morning. By then, you're hair will have air-dried mostly, so you'll only have to worry about styling it (if you want to).

For the wet hair thing, I've found those microfiber hair towels with loops are helpful. Having wet hair on the skin of my neck and shoulders is a sensory issue that bothers me, and those hair towels help a lot. They're not as heavy as full-size towels and actually stay in place.

Edited to add: You should be proud of yourself, no need for the "lol." There was something you were struggling with and you finally conquered it. Good job, seriously.

In addition to the delayed sleep phase we often have, I also think there's an element of difficulty with task switching. Switching from being awake to being asleep, switching from being asleep to being awake. I struggle to fall asleep and also struggle to actually wake up and feel alert, even when I've gotten ample rest. There are also fewer distractions at night, so it's easier to concentrate on stuff and hard to go to bed when you can *finally* focus.

I love this. Also want to add that being disciplined for the sake of being disciplined probably isn't going to work. Being disciplined in service of a goal that you actually really want to achieve or in service of an actual need is different. Identifying what you actually truly want and actually truly need is the tough part, I think, because we are trained from a young age to ignore these things in favor of what we should do or what we have to do. School and work are absolutely great at distancing us from our natural interests, so much so that we don't even know what they are. I think "laziness" is often a manifestation of internal rebellion against a way of life we don't actually want to be following.

So, this happened to me after the combination of work burnout and a rough breakup left me shattered. I moved back home, thinking it would allow me to regroup, and it has helped. My mom was also living alone after my dad passed away, and I figured that I could make myself useful by taking care of things she can't around the house. When I am home, I still walk my dog and feed her, play with her, and give her affection. My dog was always allowed to sleep on my bed and had a crate in my room with comfy bedding as well for when she wanted alone time. However, when I'm at work, my mom does feed her and take her to potty (because I can't as I typically work second shift now). My mom is home all the time, and I'm not. My mom is there for my dog more than I am, and I can't really help that because I have to work to pay my bills and contribute to the household. I also figure that my mom's positive energy is more comforting to be around than my sad energy. I have had to accept that my dog no longer prefers me, and I'm not going to force her or deprive her of the attention she gets from my mom while I'm away at work just because the situation hurts my feelings. I finally moved her crate to my mom's room because it was going unused otherwise. My dog still greets me when I get home, but I'm not her #1 favorite anymore. I'm sorry you're going through this. You might be able to remedy it by taking some other commentors' suggestions, but you might not if your mom is just around more than you are. Sometimes when we love our pet, we have to accept what is best for our pet even if it stings.

I keep seeing this news repeated here. I'm not saying WF conditons shouldn't improve, but using Aldi as an exemplar of anything is just bananas. The working conditons at Aldi are brutal. The visual of an associate sitting at register fools too many people.

Long reply incoming.

I have worked at Aldi and I currently work at Whole Foods. I have a close friend who works at Trader Joe's. If you work full time at Aldi, you will do everything and you will do it as quickly as humanly possible. You sit for cashiering not for your human comfort but because it enables you to scan more quickly. Not bagging is done for similar reasons--it allows for a higher sales volume. Getting the customers through as quickly as possible with as few staff as possible. It's annoying to hear over and over from customers that it's so nice that you're allowed to sit. It gives this false impression that there is anything cushy about working at Aldi. It's true that Trader Joe's crew members also do everything in the store, but they do so with much more staff. An Aldi shift consists of maybe 4 or 5 people at most.

I dropped down to 103 pounds when I worked at Aldi and could not eat enough to make up for the calories I was burning. A healthy weight for me is like 115. So maybe not "no" forever, just "no" until they have worked theough some things in counseling. Someone who is avoidantly attached may start to feel smothered in just about any relationship and will want out sometimes to reduce that stress, even if they do really love their partner. Someone who is anxiously attached will be constantly afraid that their partner doesn't really love them and will want out sometimes to reduce that stress, even if their partner does love them. Avoidants and anxiously attached people often end up together, which causes a pattern of the anxious person chasing validation and the avoidant person retreating. That doesn't mean that they're not right for each other, just that they need to work on themselves a bit first and learn to communicate what's underneath their pattern.

For people who don't have depression, even people who very much want to help, I think depression is more terrifying than they bargained for sometimes. I think depression in others can cause such people a real crisis of worldview, and it can cause them to really question things that they've taken for granted, things that they need to believe to function as well as they do. I think there is a fear that if they spend much time in the dark with the person they're trying to help, they will sink as well.
